Q: Autofilling data based on shared URL in Google Forms / Google Spreadsheets A:

You can create prefilled URLs that open the form so that some of the fields have a value filled in automatically. You'll need to create a URLs for each location ID. When the user opens the URL in a web browser through the QR code that uses that URL, the form opens, and the location ID is already filled in.

The answer field in the location ID question will by default be visible to the user, and they can edit it at will. To hide the location ID field, place it in a section, and skip that section.

See Send a form with pre-filled answers and Skip sections in your form.

Q: Autocomplete text color overridden when browser spellcheck activates in shadcn Input A:

When the browser detects a misspelling and applies the red squiggly line, it often forces a repaint of the text element. During this repaint, the browser tends to ignore your custom -webkit-text-fill-color and falls back to its default user-agent style (which is black text) because the "spellcheck" state doesn't inherit the "autofill" pseudo-properties correctly.

Here are the two ways to solve this.

Solution 1: The "Force" Method (CSS Fix)

You need to force the browser to respect your color text fill by adding !important to your existing CSS. The spellcheck renderer is aggressive, so your CSS specificity needs to be higher.

Update your globals.css rule to look like this:

CSS

input:-webkit-autofill,
input:-webkit-autofill:hover,
input:-webkit-autofill:focus,
input:-webkit-autofill:active {
  /* Keep your existing transition hack for the background */
  -webkit-box-shadow: 0 0 0 1000px transparent inset;
  transition: background-color 9999s ease-in-out 0s;
  
  /* ADD !important HERE */
  -webkit-text-fill-color: /* your-color-here */ !important;
}

Why this helps: The browser's default stylesheet for spellchecked words has high specificity. Adding !important prevents the browser from reverting to black when the red underline appears.

Solution 2: The Functional Fix (Disable Spellcheck)

If the CSS fix above does not work (WebKit bugs can sometimes be stubborn against even !important), the most reliable fix is to disable spellcheck on that specific input.

Since this usually happens on fields like "Email", "Username", or "Address"—where standard dictionary spellchecking isn't actually useful—disabling it is often the better UX choice anyway.

In your Shadcn/React component:

TypeScript

<Input 
  type="email" 
  placeholder="Email" 
  spellCheck={false}  // <-- Add this prop
/>

Summary

  1. Try adding !important to your -webkit-text-fill-color property in globals.css first.

  2. If that fails, or if the field doesn't strictly require spellchecking (like a login ID), set spellCheck={false} on the component.

Q: How to run multiple statistical distributions across all possible combinations of values in a column & assign the minimum to a new column? A:

...but that produces both a sample size warning

A lot of these statistical tests have no definition, or an extremely strange definition, for 0 or 1 samples.

For example, if a = 2, and b = 1, then the step

d[d['TpD'].between(a,b)].Output

will not match any rows. Then, it will evaluate what the mean value of zero elements is, and evaluate what the KS test result for a distribution of zero elements compared to an ECDF of zero elements. None of these have any sensible meaning.

For that reason, I would suggest skipping the calculation when d[d['TpD'].between(a,b)].Output contains 0 rows.

for a in d.TpD:
    
    test = pd.DataFrame()
    test['TpD'] = d['TpD'].drop_duplicates().sort_values(ascending=True).reset_index(drop=True)
    KSS = []

    for b in test.TpD:
        del KSS_elem
        subset = d[d['TpD'].between(a,b)].Output
        if len(subset) == 0:
            KSS_elem = np.nan
        else:
            Rng = stat.ecdf(subset).cdf.quantiles
            Emp = stat.ecdf(subset).cdf.probabilities
            Exp = stat.expon.cdf(Rng, 0, Rng.mean())
            KSS_elem = stat.kstest(Emp,Exp).statistic
        KSS.append(KSS_elem)

    test['KSS'] = KSS
    # bins.append(...)

If you have one element, the calculation you are trying to do technically has a meaning. But it's quite a strange meaning. If both have exactly one element, and Emp[0] == Exp[0], then the KS statistic is 0. If they differ, even by the smallest possible amount, the statistic is 1.

For this reason, I would suggest establishing some minimum number of samples where the test starts to produce reasonable results.

You could modify the previous example to something like this, to exclude 0, 1, or 2 sample KS tests.

        if len(subset) < 3:
            KSS_elem = np.nan

This would skip running a number of statistical tests that have no chance of being a good fit.

for the three lines generating the distributions and a Key Error on the last line.

Let's discuss this line:

bins.append(test[test.KSS.min()].TpD)

The specific kind of indexing you're using here (using test[...]) expects either a column name.

The KSS value you are using does not match this, so you get the KeyError.

(Note: in this example, because you used reset_index(), the numbers are integers going in order. But this is not generally true for all indexes.)

There are generally two ways to fix this.

  1. You could fix this by obtaining the int position of the smallest value, rather than the value itself.

    bins.append(test.iloc[test.KSS.argmin()].TpD)

    Note: argmin returns the integer position of the row (used with .iloc[]) not the index of the row (used with .loc[].) Here, it doesn't matter, but if your index labels are not in order, then it does.

  2. Alternatively, for a more elegant but slower solution, you could try sorting the dataframe by KSS. This will put the TpD value you are interested in in the first row. To access the first element, you can get the first value in the TpD column.

    bins.append(test.sort_values('KSS').TpD.iloc[0])

Either solution would work here.

Broadly, in summary, I would suggest a solution along these lines:

import scipy
import scipy.stats as stat
import numpy as np
import random
import string
import pandas as pd


def gen_data():
    N = 100
    ret = {
        'Locations': [
            ''.join(random.choice(string.ascii_uppercase) for _ in range(3))
            for i in range(N)
        ],
        'TpD': scipy.stats.expon.rvs(scale=5, size=N),
        'out_init': scipy.stats.uniform.rvs(size=N) + 1,
    }
    ret = pd.DataFrame(ret)
    ret['Output'] = ret['TpD'] * ret['out_init'] * 1000
    ret = ret.drop(columns=['out_init'])
    return ret

def question_example():
    Location = ['CIL', 'BUR', 'SNA', 'PRT'] #a 3-letter code for each unique location data is recorded
    TpD = [2.0, 6.5, 32.0, 2.86] #the average number of times per day an event occurs at that location (the independent variable)
    Output = [3685, 58492, 285938, 10491] #the total recorded output produced by those events over a year (the dependent variable)

    d=pd.DataFrame({'Location': Location, 'TpD': TpD, 'Output': Output})
    return d

def get_bins(d):
    bins = []
    d_sorted = d.sort_values('TpD').set_index('TpD').Output
    for a in d.TpD:
        test = pd.DataFrame()
        test['TpD'] = d['TpD'].drop_duplicates().sort_values(ascending=True).reset_index(drop=True)
        KSS = []

        for b in test.TpD:
            if a > b:
                # No elements can match a <= x <= b.
                subset = []
            else:
                subset = d_sorted[a:b].values
            if len(subset) < 3:
                KSS_elem = np.nan
            else:
                Rng = np.sort(subset)
                Emp = np.arange(1, len(subset) + 1) / len(subset)
                Exp = stat.expon.cdf(Rng, 0, Rng.mean())
                KSS_elem = stat.kstest(Emp,Exp).statistic
            KSS.append(KSS_elem)

        test['KSS'] = KSS
        if not pd.isna(test.KSS).all():
            bins.append(test.iloc[test.KSS.argmin()].TpD)
        else:
            bins.append(np.nan)
    return np.array(bins)


d_val = gen_data()
# d_val = question_example()
d_val['bins'] = get_bins(d_val)
d_val

On the one hand, it would be nice if I could fix the specific errors in this script so that I know what I'm doing wrong. On the other hand, there surely has to be a way to do this that doesn't require for loops.

I can't think of any existing library functions for doing what you're trying to do. It's a fairly niche thing to do, so you'll have to code it yourself.

From a speed perspective, I took a quick attempt at optimizing the code. (See above.) It spends most of its time inside stat.kstest(). This part is not going to be fast, since it needs to run this O(n^2) times. Also, a KS test, like most nonparametric tests, is fairly slow.

I would suggest considering a faster alternative, like scipy.stats.anderson(). This allows you to directly compare a datasample to a theoretical CDF. This would also allow you to skip obtaining an ECDF. However, the results from this won't be exactly the same as a KS test. I don't understand the purpose of your statistical test, so I can't comment on whether this is important.

Q: Populate Google Apps flexTable with filtered Spreadsheet Data and returning changes to spreadsheet A:

flextables are not working like spreadsheets, you can't get widgets values directly as part of the table. You have to get every textBox and checkBox separately using e.parameter.Name.

You can do that easily in a loop but you'll have to know the number of textBoxes to be able to rebuild the names just as you did to create them in the doGet function.

I would suggest to store this number in a tag on one of your widget or in a separate hidden widget (hidden class or invisible textBox). Then you will be able to get the values like this :

...
var results = [];// an array to collect results
var numberOfItems = Number(e.parameter.itemNumbers); // this is the var you are missing right now and need to add. This is the solution of a separate hidden widget
for(var n=0;n<numberOfItems;n++){
  results.push([e.parameter['hours'+n],e.parameter['complete'+n]]);// each element is an array of 2 values
  }
... // from here you will have an 2D array with all your values and you can continue like you did=.
